sources.title: Friday Photo Tip | Joints
sources.author: Amanda Lessner
sources.identity: Oahu family photographer; her bio says she has photographed families for 16 years and her site offers portrait/family sessions
sources.kind: professional photographer tip with annotated comparison examples
sources.trust_reason: First-party working photographer gives a named, practical portrait cropping method with captioned comparisons; professional bio independently on her own site describes 16 years photographing families.
sources.read_depth: Read the full article and the author bio. Text and image captions identify knee/ankle/joint and adjacent-segment crop comparisons; example pixels were not opened.
sources.notes: The article makes a categorical “never crop at joints” statement. Use only as one photographer’s recommendation; do not promote that wording as a universal rule. Captions describe the linked demonstrations; no pixel-level visual review was performed.

sources.title: Portrait Crop: The Ultimate Guide to Cropping Portraits Like a Pro (original title: Good Crop Bad Crop – How to Crop Portraits)
sources.author: Gina Milicia
sources.identity: Professional portrait photographer for 25+ years; dPS bio states she photographed high-profile people and runs workshops and private mentoring
sources.kind: professional photographer tutorial published by photography education site
coverage: cropping at knees and other joints
sources.trust_reason: Named working portrait photographer with extensive professional experience and teaching record; complete tutorial includes her rationale, image comparisons and an explicit section on deliberate crops and breaking rules.
sources.read_depth: Read complete article sections on in-camera crops, joint cuts, crop alternatives, deliberate crops and the author bio. Linked images are present but their pixels were not opened.
sources.notes: Gina recommends avoiding joint crops as a starting point but explicitly says crops need individual judgment and the rule can be broken deliberately. Do not record “never crop a knee” as a universal law.

sources.title: Portretfotografie tip: Draai de camera (Portrait photography tip: Rotate the camera)
sources.author: Elja Trum
sources.identity: Portrait photographer, photography educator and author; Photofacts bio says he has written about photography since 2006 and authored books on portrait photography, composition and flash
sources.kind: portrait-photographer tutorial published by photography education site
coverage: camera roll / Dutch angle in portrait
sources.trust_reason: Named portrait photographer and educator explains a specific portrait camera-roll technique; full Dutch original is open and author qualifications are stated on the page.
sources.read_depth: Read complete Dutch article and author bio; inspected text/captions only, not the linked example image pixels.
sources.notes: The author claims 30–45 degrees often looks intentional and 5–10 degrees can look accidental. This is a single photographer’s numerical method and directly conflicts with Nikon’s much smaller portrait-tilt advice; preserve the disagreement and do not derive a numeric rule.

sources.title: How to nail portrait photography as a beginner
sources.author: Nikon Team
sources.identity: Nikon Europe editorial team; the linked author profile says the team works with Nikon Ambassadors and Creators across Europe
sources.trust_reason: Official Nikon Europe portrait tutorial has full text, captions and a team identity with stated contributor access.
sources.read_depth: Read the full article and Nikon Team profile; Dutch tilt and viewpoint sections were checked. Linked image pixels were not opened.
sources.notes: Nikon suggests a slight tilt for dynamic portrait feel and cautions against more than about 5–10 degrees. This conflicts with Elja Trum’s 30–45-degree suggestion; record as differing methods, not averaged guidance.

gaps: Independent portrait photography sources for Dutch tilt agree that roll can be a deliberate compositional variable, but they conflict on useful angles (Elja Trum: larger tilt for clear intention; Nikon Europe: keep it slight). There is no defensible universal degree threshold or tested rule for cosplay stills.

A film textbook explains that Dutch angle can signal imbalance/chaos and that high/low-angle meanings depend on scene context, but this does not establish a universal still-portrait or cosplay interpretation. More named portrait-photographer examples tying body pose, background verticals and tilt to a specific intended effect would improve coverage.

Two named portrait photographers discuss joint-adjacent cropping, including knees, and one explicitly permits deliberate exceptions. Current evidence supports comparing crop choices, not a categorical ban. A controlled or independently documented comparison focused on different poses, motion, costume and intentional abstraction remains absent.

The new sources are general portrait/family photography, Nikon editorial and cinematography; none address cosplay costume construction, posed action, armor, skirts or convention constraints. Keep such applications as project-designed tests.
